examples.explain: 3 appears four times, 1 three times, 5 once.

hints: Start by counting. Once you know every value's frequency, the question is just "which k counts are biggest?"
Sorting the distinct values by count is O(n log n). A size-k min-heap gets you to O(n log k).
A frequency is an integer between 1 and n. Use it as an index: bucket[f] = values seen f times.

insight.mnemonic: When the key is a small integer, index by it instead of sorting by it.
insight.oneLiner: Count, then index buckets by frequency (frequencies are bounded by n) and read them from the top down.

recall.a: Min-heap of size k: the root is the weakest of the current top k, so it's the one to evict.
recall.q: Heap approach: min-heap or max-heap, and why?

recall.a: Frequencies are integers in [1, n], so n + 1 buckets cover every possibility.
recall.q: Why does bucket sort work here?

insight.why: Bucket sort is linear because the 'keys' (frequencies) live in the small range 1..n.

oneLiner: Count, then index buckets by frequency (frequencies are bounded by n) and read them from the top down.

pitfalls.explain: Check your sort direction or heap type - a min-heap pops the *smallest* frequency first.
pitfalls.title: Returned the least frequent values

pitfalls.explain: The answer is the values themselves, not how often they appear.
pitfalls.title: Returned frequencies instead of values

solutions.idea: Count with a hash map, sort the distinct values by count, take k.
solutions.name: Count, then sort

solutions.idea: Keep only the k best candidates in a min-heap; evict the smallest whenever it grows past k.
solutions.name: Size-k min-heap

footnotes.text: A frequency can never exceed len(nums), so there are only n + 1 possible buckets. Indexing by frequency replaces sorting.

solutions.idea: Frequencies are bounded by n, so bucket values by frequency and read buckets from high to low.
solutions.name: Bucket sort by frequency

starter:
class Solution:
    def topKFrequent(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> List[int]:
statement:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` values that **appear most often**. The answer may be in any order.

The input guarantees the answer is unique - there is never a tie at the k-th place.
title: Top K Frequent Elements
